extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on examination and drafting of patent claims, focusing on indefiniteness, mixed-category claims, product-by-process, use/omnibus claims, claim interpretation, chemical and trademark claim issues, and compact prosecution practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple inclusion (double inclusion) of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the facts in each case to determine whether the multiple inclusion of one or more elements in a claim gives rise to indefiniteness in that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply automatic rules for or against 'double inclusion'; the governing consideration is what is a reasonable construction of the claim language (In re Kelly). A compound embraced by more than one member of a Markush group does not by itself create uncertainty as to claim scope, but a device claim that can be read to include the same element twice may be indefinite (Ex parte Kristensen). Apply older cases (Ex parte White, Ex parte Clark) with care according to case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A product-by-process claim, which is a product claim that defines the claimed product in terms of the process by which it is made, is proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product-by-process claiming is permissible (Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma; In re Luck; In re Pilkington; In re Steppan). A claim to a device, apparatus, manufacture, or composition may reference the process in which it is intended to be used without objection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) so long as it is clear the claim is directed to the product and not the process. Applicants may present claims of varying scope even if description in product-by-process terms is necessary (Ex parte Pantzer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and process in the same claim (mixed apparatus/method)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single claim that claims both an apparatus and the method steps of using the apparatus is indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a system claim contains limitations that are actions of users (i.e., not directed to the system), it creates confusion as to when infringement occurs and is indefinite (In re Katz Interactive Call Processing Patent Litigation; IPXL Holdings v. Amazon.com). Ex parte Lyell held a claim that combined an automatic transmission workstand and the method of using it ambiguous and properly rejected. By contrast, if additional limitations focus on the capabilities of the system (not specific user actions), the claim may be definite (Mastermine Software, Inc. v. Microsoft Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Use" claims (claims reciting mere use without steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempts to claim a process without setting forth any steps (mere 'use') generally raise an indefiniteness issue under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and may fail to claim statutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that simply recite a use without active, positive steps delimiting how the use is practiced can be held indefinite (Ex parte Erlich). Claims that do not purport to claim a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter fail to comply with 35 U.S.C. 101 (In re Moreton). Examples of improper 'use' claim wording and case outcomes are provided (Ex parte Dunki; Clinical Products Ltd. v. Brenner). Procedurally, a claim reciting a use but failing to recite steps may be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 (form paragraph 7.05.01) and/or as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (form paragraph 7.34.01). Note: in some instances a recited step such as 'utilizing' was held not indefinite (Ex parte Porter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import specification limitations into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a claim should be interpreted in light of the specification disclosure, it is generally improper to read limitations contained in the specification into the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and courts should not rely on the specification to impart limitations to the claim that are not recited in the claim (In re Prater; In re Winkhaus). Interpretation must respect the claim language as written.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omnibus claims are indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims such as 'A device substantially as shown and described' (omnibus claims) are indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omnibus claims fail to point out what is included or excluded by the claim language and are properly rejected (Ex parte Fressola). Such a claim can be rejected using form paragraph 7.35; see MPEP § 2175 for history and explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to figures or tables in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be complete in themselves; incorporation by reference to a specific figure or table is permitted only in exceptional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporation by reference into a claim is allowed only where there is no practical way to define the invention in words and where incorporating by reference is more concise — a 'necessity doctrine,' not for applicant convenience (Ex parte Fressola). Reference characters from the detailed description and drawings may be used in claims; generally presence or absence of such characters does not affect claim scope. See MPEP § 608.01(m) for treatment of reference characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical formula/structure claims and definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims to chemical compounds or compositions using formulas or partial structures are not necessarily indefinite in the absence of evidence that the assigned formula is in error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not find chemical structure claims indefinite merely because a structure is not fully presented or corroborating spectroscopic data is absent (Ex parte Morton; Ex parte Sobin). A claim to a chemical compound with partial structure or with wording like 'polypeptide of at least 24 amino acids having the following sequence' may be broad but not indefinite (In re Fisher). Compounds may be claimed by a name that adequately describes the material to one skilled in the art (Martin v. Johnson). Unknown structures may be claimed by a combination of physical and chemical characteristics (Ex parte Brian). A compound may also be claimed in product-by-process terms without raising indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks or trade names in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a trademark or trade name in a claim is not per se improper, but the claim must be analyzed to determine how the mark or name is used and whether it renders the claim indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trademark identifies a source of goods and does not define the goods themselves (see MPEP § 608.01(v)). If a trademark/trade name is used as a limitation to identify or describe a particular material or product, the claim does not comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (Ex parte Simpson). If present but not intended as a limitation, the reason for its inclusion should be addressed; if it causes confusion as to scope, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). If an applicant replaces a trade name with a generic term, the examiner should determine whether there is sufficient support in the application for the generic term (see MPEP § 2163). Example: Examiner rejection of 'ALIMTA' as indefinite (Eli Lilly & Co. v. Apotex, Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere function of a machine is not sole ground for rejection of process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Process or method claims should not be rejected solely because they define an inherent function of a disclosed machine or apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process claim that is otherwise patentable should not be rejected merely because the application discloses an apparatus that will inherently carry out the recited steps (In re Tarczy-Hornoch). Examiners should not use the mere fact of inherent machine function as the sole basis for a 35 U.S.C. 112(b) rejection of process claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution: interpret claims and state indefiniteness interpretation early
rubrics_metrics.description: Under compact prosecution, the examiner should review claims for all statutory requirements early and clearly articulate any rejection and the interpretation of indefinite terms in the first Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal is to articulate rejections early so applicant can timely respond with evidence of patentability (see MPEP § 706; 37 CFR 1.104(a)(1)). When a claim term renders the claim indefinite, the examiner should make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and also make any rejection(s) under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103 that apply based on the examiner's interpretation of the claim. The examiner must state on the record how a claim term or phrase is being interpreted with respect to the prior art applied, thereby avoiding piecemeal examination (see In re Packard; MPEP § 707.07(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art rejection practice when claim is indefinite (two-approach guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When terms of a claim are considered indefinite, determine whether to also reject over prior art depending on the degree of uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach 1 (recommended when uncertainty is not great): Enter two rejections — (A) indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) and (B) a rejection over the prior art based on the interpretation that renders the claim unpatentable; when making the prior art rejection, point out how the claim is being interpreted (Ex parte Ionescu). Approach 2 (when there is great confusion/uncertainty): Do not base a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection on considerable speculation about claim meaning or assumptions about scope (In re Steele). The first approach avoids piecemeal examination and may give applicants better appreciation of relevant prior art if claims are redrafted.
